prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are a clean example of a new measurement technique that opened new physics. Magic-wavelength trapping lets thousands of atoms be interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil shifts, and fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 have been reached. The idea (Katori) and the realisation at the accuracy frontier (Ye) are separable and well documented. The result has been reproduced and surpassed by several independent groups (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and others), and clock comparisons are now routine. The consequences are concrete: millimetre-scale relativistic redshift measurements, tests of constants and dark-matter searches, and the pending redefinition of the second. Seven of eight members rank it, and it has the highest first-place count and Borda total on the shortlist. The two-name configuration is cleaner than any other shortlisted candidate, and the field is mature without being stale.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is priority and overlap. The 2005 prize (Hall, Hansch) covered the frequency comb that makes optical clocks usable as clockwork, and the 2012 prize (Wineland) covered ion clocks, so the committee must be convinced that the lattice clock is a distinct achievement and not a continuation of the same line. Other lattice-clock contributors (Lemonde, Gill, Bloom, Ludlow and others) could also be argued for, and Ye's group results are partly built on the comb and cavity-stabilisation work of the Hall lineage. Finally, the largest payoffs, a redefined second and geodesy or dark-matter results, are still ahead, so a sceptic could call the impact promised rather than delivered. I am not fully persuaded that this last point should weigh against a demonstrated measurement capability, but it is a fair point.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a clean demonstration of controllable quantum physics on a chip that became the architecture of superconducting processors, and calls it the natural next step after the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I agree that circuit QED is mature and scientifically strong, and I ranked it third myself. But I read the 2025 prize as the reason for caution rather than a reason for urgency: two circuit-based recognitions in two years would need a distinct justification, and the 2004 theory and first strong-coupling experiment sit in the same line of macroscopic quantum circuits. You also note that Girvin and Devoret are missing from the credited trio, and the credit is more entangled with Yale, Delft and Zurich than for the clock case. Where we may differ is on what the field has delivered for physics itself: lattice clocks have already given a measurement (millimetre redshift, 1e-18) that no other instrument gives. I would keep circuit QED as my first alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, since a quantitative band-theory prediction was followed by experimental demonstration of correlated insulators and superconductivity, and he considers the core discovery stable and timely.
responses.response: I take the prediction-then-experiment argument seriously, and Bistritzer-MacDonald plus Jarillo-Herrero is a tidy configuration. My reservation is the one you partly share and Johansson, Lindroth and Olsson state more strongly: the field is eight years old, the origin of the superconductivity is unsettled, and sample-to-sample reproducibility is still a recognised issue. From an experimentalist's view I would also want the measured phenomenology to be controlled before a prize fixes the narrative. It is also a field where I am no expert, so I defer to you on the condensed-matter depth, but I do not think the maturity gap relative to a clock that has been compared across continents can be waved away. I would not object strongly if the committee preferred it, but it is not my choice.

responses.point: Lindroth also ranks optical lattice clocks first, calling it precision atomic physics at its best, with a clear idea, close agreement of theory and experiment and an unforeseen payoff, and she regards the credit as not seriously disputed.
responses.response: I agree on the physics and on Katori and Ye, but I would qualify the claim that credit is undisputed. Lemonde, Gill and Bloom (SYRTE, NPL and NIST) made real contributions to the lattice-clock line, and the committee should check this against the primary record before we assume the pair is uncontroversial. I also want us to be explicit that the case rests on the lattice clock, not on the comb, which was already honoured; the citation should say so. Your point that this is a prize with a payoff nobody foresaw is, to me, the strongest reason to prefer it over the incremental proposals on the list.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as an instrument-driven new window on cosmic-ray accelerators and ranks optical lattice clocks fifth, while noting that the Halzen-Karle-Spiering attribution is hard to settle.
responses.response: Your criterion, that instruments opening a new window weigh most, is one I share, so I take IceCube seriously. My difficulty is attribution and maturity: the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND lineage makes the three-person cut awkward, as you admit yourself, and source identification (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) is still firming up with KM3NeT confirmation developing. Lattice clocks are the opposite case: two clearly separable contributors, independent confirmation by many labs and a stable interpretation. I also note you agree that the pair is compact and well defined. I would put IceCube behind the clock case today, though I would be willing to revisit it if colleagues can establish who was decisive for the 2013 evidence.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes.
Whether other lattice-clock pioneers (for example Lemonde, Gill, Bloom) have a claim that a two-name prize would unfairly exclude; the primary priority record should be checked.
How much weight to give the fact that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened.
Whether circuit QED can be separated cleanly enough from the 2025 prize to be a serious competitor this year.
statement.conflict_note: I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory during my PhD, and Hall's JILA group is the lineage in which Jun Ye worked, so there is a mentor-lineage connection to one proposed laureate, although I have no direct collaboration with Ye or Katori that I know of. I am an atomic physicist and share the broad field, and I lead quantum-sensing work in WACQT, a Chalmers-led centre that overlaps institutionally with Johansson's home institution; B013 is Johansson's first choice. I flag these for the committee's judgement on recusal. No other specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile.
